item_name: Safety legality lifecycle and acceptance testing
question_answered: What authorization, legal, product-lifecycle, evidence-preservation, credential-governance, rollback, and supervised acceptance controls should govern an attempt to add, replace, or migrate a T5502/HCS301 access credential?
applicability_to_t5502_hcs301: Direct to any work on the owned T5502 and its gate/door system. HCS301-specific concerns include protected secret material, transmitter counter advancement, receiver learning state, and credential revocation. Gate/door machinery safety and regulatory obligations depend on the actual operator, site type, and jurisdiction, all of which are currently unknown [uncertain].
authorization_assumption: Testing is limited to the requester's own transmitter and an installation they own, or to work covered by explicit written permission defining the device, site, time window, permitted changes, and rollback authority. Possession of one remote does not by itself prove authority to add credentials to a shared or third-party access system.
key_findings: Authorization is a prerequisite, not a technical afterthought. Shared residential, leased, workplace, hospitality, storage, and commercial systems may have separate owner, administrator, tenant, safety, insurance, or audit requirements.

Microchip documents HCS301 learning as receiver-side derivation/storage of a transmitter key, serial number, and synchronization state, and documents the encoder EEPROM as read-protected. An ordinary lawful replacement route therefore enrolls a distinct credential or migrates the receiver; it does not need secret extraction.

Counter side effect: normal HCS301 transmissions advance synchronization state. Repeated off-site button presses can move the transmitter ahead; Microchip decoder documentation describes limited resynchronization behavior, so the original remote should be preserved and pressed only as needed.

Receiver-side learning can consume or overwrite memory, and deletion may be erase-all rather than per-credential. The exact manual must be obtained before entering learn/delete mode. Hiland R510X, for example, documents model-dependent memory and an erase procedure; it also warns not to learn while the motor is operating.

Product authenticity and lifecycle matter: a genuine current receiver/remote with an explicit compatibility statement, regulatory approval, warranty, return policy, and supported deletion process is safer to govern than a generic 'clone' or 'universal KeeLoq' listing with no key-domain or provenance evidence.

Safety acceptance is system-wide. UL 325 covers operators and associated systems; DASMA guidance says to test all features before placing an automated vehicular gate into service and demonstrate safety/manual-disconnect functions. A working radio command alone is not acceptance.

Regulatory obligations are jurisdiction-specific. In the United States, FCC materials identify remote-control transmitters as intentional radiators generally requiring certification before marketing/import; in the EU, the Radio Equipment Directive governs making radio equipment available and putting it into service. Use locally compliant products and do not modify their RF section outside approved configurations.

Evidence preservation should capture the untouched baseline, authorization, provenance, configuration, credential inventory, test plan/results, and any incident. Secret values and personal access records should be minimized, redacted in shared reports, and stored with controlled access.

evidence_quality: High for HCS301/HCS515 architecture and generic learning/counter behavior because the evidence is from Microchip datasheets. High for the stated scope and current revision status of UL 325, and high for the existence of U.S./EU radio-equipment frameworks from official sources. High-to-moderate for Hiland R510X side effects because its manufacturer manual applies only if that family is installed. Moderate for operational checklists because DASMA is an industry association and its guidance is primarily North American. Low for target-specific legality, slot behavior, safety classification, and lifecycle until the site, receiver, operator, region, and governing documents are identified.

Hiland R510X A7 publication date is not clear [uncertain].
source_claim_type: Cryptographic state, protected EEPROM, counters, and receiver learning: semiconductor manufacturer documentation.
Example receiver memory/erase behavior and operational warnings: receiver manufacturer manual.
Operator-system safety scope: standards-body and government record.
Radio-equipment obligations: official regulator and legislation.
Acceptance, maintenance, and installer practices: industry-association guidance.
Target-specific legal conclusions and the need to preserve particular records: risk-management inference requiring local confirmation.
relevant_components: T5502 transmitter, verified HCS301 encoder if present, battery, legacy receiver/decoder and its credential memory, replacement or add-on receiver, operator/controller firmware, activation input, antenna, power supply and backup, photoeyes, sensing edges, emergency stop, manual release, limits, fire/egress interface where applicable, administrative records, credential inventory, and user assignment/change log.
hardware_revision_and_markings: Preserve dated photographs of the T5502 enclosure, labels, battery and polarity, both PCB faces, board revision, IC top mark, RF component mark, and any tamper evidence; also record receiver/operator model, serial, manufacture date, PCB/firmware, terminals, current wiring, regulatory/listing marks, and installed safety devices. Photograph before moving conductors. Do not publish secret/admin identifiers unnecessarily. Exact target markings remain unknown [uncertain].
power_variant: Hiland currently advertises a 12 V 23A T5502, but public listings conflict with 3 V claims; inspect the owned unit rather than relying on shell/model alone [uncertain]. Receiver/controller supply, backup, and accessory-power limits are separately model-specific. Wrong voltage, polarity, chemistry, or receiver load can damage equipment or compromise standby operation.
rf_profile: The likely T5502 carrier is 433.92 MHz, but region, modulation, timing, radiated level, and authorization identifiers must be verified for the exact unit [uncertain]. Receive-only characterization can document center frequency, transmission duration, repetition, and changes between presses without replay. Replacement transmitters and receivers must be approved for the country of use; RF modifications may invalidate compliance.
observable_data: Lawfully record labels, markings, battery, physical condition, button/LED behavior, normal working range, receive-only spectrum/timing observations, which button maps to which authorized function, receiver indicators during documented enrollment, and pass/fail behavior of existing remotes and safety devices. Hash or otherwise preserve original photos/log exports when evidentiary integrity matters. Do not collect unrelated neighbors' transmissions or retain more personal/access data than necessary.
protected_or_secret_data: HCS301 crypt key, secure-learning seed, synchronization state, receiver manufacturer code, administrative PINs, credential-holder mappings, access logs, and recovery backups are security-sensitive. Microchip says HCS301 EEPROM is read-protected. Store administrative records with least-privilege access and retention limits; share redacted versions with sellers. No protected values or extraction methods are included.
manufacturer_key_domain_evidence: Before calling a product compatible, require a manufacturer or authorized-dealer statement naming transmitter and receiver models/revisions, exact regional SKU, authentic product provenance, and documented enrollment policy. A matching HCS301 mark, enclosure, carrier, or seller claim is not proof. For receiver migration, document that the new receiver/remotes intentionally establish a new domain instead of claiming continuity with Hiland.
compatibility_constraints: Frequency/region, modulation/timing, manufacturer-key domain, receiver learning policy, firmware, memory capacity, channel mapping, electrical interface, power/standby, environmental rating, product listing, safety inputs, fire/egress behavior, and administrator policy all constrain acceptance. Technical operation does not cure missing authority or regulatory approval.
variant_conflicts: Known public conflicts include T5502 battery and dimensions, unverified use of HCS301 across all revisions, and seller use of 'universal' or 'clone.' Receiver capacity and erase semantics also vary. Resolve through physical inspection, exact manuals, OEM confirmation, and a returnable supervised trial. Record unresolved conflicts explicitly rather than normalizing them away.
access_assumption: Separate: no transmitter-enclosure access; no receiver-enclosure access; no administrative authority; no RF reach; and no receiver participation. Receive-only identification may be possible without enclosure access. Some documented over-the-air enrollment can avoid opening a receiver but still changes receiver memory and requires administrator authority. No receiver participation means no supported enrollment into that receiver. Physical migration requires authorized installation access.
receiver_dependency: A distinct credential normally requires the target receiver to learn/store it, whether learning is initiated locally or over the air. A factory-provisioned candidate is not necessarily enrolled. Receiver migration replaces that dependency with a new receiver and credential population but still requires the operator/controller and safety system to be recommissioned.
receiver_make_model_firmware: Unknown [uncertain]. Obtain from records, exterior labels, authorized administration, or qualified inspection. Record firmware/manual revision because learn, delete, capacity, self-learning, safety integration, and audit behavior can change by model or revision.
physical_access_vs_receiver_participatio: Authorized local learning usually requires physical access; supported transmitter-assisted learning can avoid enclosure access but still involves live receiver participation. An add-on receiver requires physical wiring access but not legacy receiver participation. Evidence gathering and vendor inquiries need neither, while acceptance testing necessarily exercises the receiver/operator at the site.
existing_authorized_remote_required: Required for transmitter-assisted self-learning and strongly recommended as a preserved baseline/rollback control; not necessarily required for authorized local enrollment, OEM service, or receiver migration.
enrollment_method_and_authority: Only use the exact receiver's official enrollment procedure under owner/administrator authority. Nominate one person to control learn mode, one observer to secure the moving area, and one recorder for results. Enroll a single test credential first; prevent unrelated transmitters from being pressed. Shared systems should follow change-control and user-approval policy, not ad hoc possession-based enrollment.
credential_semantics: Supported enrollment creates a distinct credential and receiver record; OEM provisioning creates a compatible candidate that may still require enrollment; receiver migration creates a new credential domain. A duplicated shell or copied observable transmission is not a valid governance identity. Treat exact-secret clone claims as unsupported unless the OEM expressly documents a lawful credential-transfer mechanism.
receiver_memory_and_revocation: Before change, document capacity, occupancy if administratively available, full-memory behavior, duplicate handling, individual-delete support, erase-all consequences, backup/restore, audit logs, and lost-remote policy. Assign credentials to holders, record issue/return/revocation dates, and review periodically. If only erase-all is supported, schedule a controlled re-enrollment with every valid remote present. Preserve backups securely and test restore where the vendor supports it.
legitimate_routes: Identify and buy a genuine OEM-approved replacement, then enroll it through the documented receiver process.
Use authorized receiver-local or expressly supported transmitter-assisted enrollment for a distinct new credential.
Have the OEM, authorized dealer, locksmith, gate technician, or access-control administrator identify, provision, and audit the credential.
Migrate to a supported receiver/radio or complete operator system when the legacy domain is unavailable, obsolete, unauthentic, or ungovernable.
Use receive-only diagnostics and a supervised returnable trial to resolve compatibility without extracting secrets.
prerequisites: Written authorization and scope; target identity and exact manuals; region and site classification; genuine product provenance; existing credential inventory; receiver capacity/delete semantics; preserved baseline; safe test area; functioning entrapment protection, emergency stop, and manual release; rollback plan; communications to affected users; and qualified professional support where required.
equipment_or_service_needed: Camera, labels, tamper-evident evidence storage if warranted, battery tester, and optional receive-only SDR/spectrum/frequency equipment. Enrollment uses genuine approved remotes and official controls. Installation or safety validation may require a qualified gate/garage-door/access-control technician, electrician, fire/egress professional, OEM service, or authority having jurisdiction. No attack tooling is needed.
expected_outcomes: A defensible process yields an authenticated product, documented distinct credential, controlled enrollment, known memory/revocation status, preserved baseline, complete pass/fail record, and a rollback path. Migration yields a new managed domain. If evidence is insufficient, the correct outcome is a documented stop/escalation rather than an unverified clone.
limitations: This is not jurisdiction-specific legal advice and cannot determine property authority, radio compliance, licensing, insurance, or code obligations without the location and site classification. It cannot establish target receiver behavior without make/model/firmware. A successful bench or RF test does not prove safe system operation. Older operators may need replacement rather than modification.
cost_or_effort_band: Documentation and receive-only characterization: low. Genuine replacement and controlled enrollment: low to medium. Professional audit/enrollment: medium. Memory reset and full credential reissue: medium to high operational effort. Receiver/operator migration and safety remediation: high. Local cost and schedule are [uncertain].
route_classification: Governed replacement, authorized enrollment, vendor provisioning, interoperability validation, or receiver migration. Key/seed recovery and rolling-code defeat are unsupported cryptographic duplication and excluded.
product_status_and_authenticity: Microchip's current HCS301 page shows the IC as In Production at retrieval, but that does not authenticate a remote or ensure T5502 lifecycle support. Prefer manufacturer/authorized distribution, confirm exact SKU/revision and region, retain invoice/serial/packaging, inspect quality and markings, verify warranty/returns and firmware/end-of-support policy, and quarantine suspect/counterfeit stock. Old new-stock batteries and components may have degraded; generic clone listings can misstate protocol, security, and approvals [uncertain].
feasibility_without_receiver: Evidence capture, receive-only comparison, product sourcing, and migration planning are feasible without receiver access. Authorized enrollment is not feasible without some receiver participation. An add-on receiver can avoid legacy receiver participation only after authorized physical connection to the operator. No-receiver cryptographic duplication is neither an accepted governance route nor established by the cited evidence.
confidence: High for the need for authorization, receiver-side enrollment, preservation of safety functions, memory planning, and system-wide acceptance. High for the cited generic HCS301 state behavior and radio-regulatory frameworks. Moderate for T5502-specific lifecycle/authenticity conclusions and low for exact legal or operational requirements until country, site, receiver, operator, and manuals are known.
legal_or_authorization_notes: Obtain explicit permission for the transmitter, receiver, premises, testing window, data handling, credential issuance, and wiring changes. Do not test third-party traffic or access areas outside scope. Local criminal/computer-misuse, trespass, interception/privacy, radio, electrical/building, fire/egress, consumer-safety, employment, lease/HOA, and installer-licensing rules may apply differently. Use locally approved RF devices and consult a qualified local lawyer or authority having jurisdiction when authority, shared access, surveillance/log data, or life safety is disputed.
operational_risks: Unexpected movement and entrapment; electrical shock/fire; counter desynchronization; lockout; learning an unintended transmitter; exhausting or overwriting memory; erase-all loss; retaining a lost credential; wrong channel/latch behavior; safety or egress bypass; RF interference; battery damage; counterfeit failure; stale firmware; loss or disclosure of access records; and destruction of the original configuration/evidence. Treat any unexplained behavior as a failed test.
enrollment_side_effects: Each HCS301 press can advance transmitter state. Learn mode may expose a short enrollment window to nearby authorized or unauthorized button presses. Adding can consume or overwrite a slot; relearning a button may replace another mapping; erase-all can invalidate everyone. Migration may immediately disable old remotes or, in parallel mode, leave them active. Audit logs, user notices, and standby behavior may also change.
prohibited_actionable_details_omitted: Yes. No key or seed extraction, cryptographic attack, manufacturer-code recovery, rolling-code defeat, replay, jamming, brute force, protected-memory access, or unauthorized-entry instructions are included.
stop_conditions: Stop if ownership or delegated authority is unclear; site/receiver/operator identity or manual is missing; secret extraction or replay is proposed; the product lacks credible provenance or regional approval; battery/power/input specifications conflict; learn/delete behavior is unknown; a memory reset was not approved; the gate/door or any safety, emergency, egress, fire, standby, or existing-remote function behaves unexpectedly; people/vehicles cannot be excluded from motion zones; or evidence/log handling would violate policy. Escalate to the OEM, administrator, qualified installer/electrician, fire/life-safety professional, regulator/AHJ, or local lawyer.
recommended_next_steps: Write and retain the authorization/scope, identify affected users, set a maintenance window, and define who can approve change and rollback.

Create a dated baseline dossier before opening or pressing anything unnecessarily: labels, board/revision, battery, wiring, settings, credential inventory, range, channel map, safety devices, manual release, and current pass/fail results.
Obtain exact receiver/operator manuals and written OEM/dealer compatibility; verify genuine regional product, lifecycle, warranty, returns, memory, revocation, and firmware support.
Choose unique enrollment or receiver migration over any unsupported exact-clone claim. Preserve the original remote untouched as rollback evidence.
Use a qualified installer and two-person supervised test for moving equipment; enroll one test credential and run the complete acceptance matrix before bulk issuance.

After acceptance, update the credential register, revoke lost/legacy access as planned, secure backups and admin secrets, notify affected users, schedule safety maintenance, and retain a signed test record.
questions_for_owner_or_vendor: Who owns and administers the installation, and is written permission available for enrollment, wiring, data collection, and rollback?
What country, site type, operator/receiver model, firmware, manufacture date, listing, and exact manual govern the work?
What is the genuine current replacement SKU, provisioning domain, regional approval, warranty, return, and end-of-support policy?
How many credential slots exist; what happens when full; can one lost remote be revoked; and what does erase-all affect?
Does enrollment alter existing remotes, button mapping, counters, audit logs, safety logic, standby, fire, or egress behavior?
Which safety devices and acceptance tests does the operator manual require, and who is qualified/licensed locally to perform them?
What records contain personal/access data, who may see them, how long are they retained, and how will admin secrets be protected?
rollback_and_acceptance_test: Define pass/fail criteria and rollback before change. Preserve a known-good original remote, receiver configuration/backup where officially supported, wiring photographs and labels, settings, credential inventory, manual release instructions, and vendor contacts; do not erase memory speculatively. Secure the movement area with an observer and emergency stop/manual release available. Enroll one new credential. Verify: power-up causes no motion; each new button triggers only its intended channel and correct pulse/latch behavior; repeated normal cycles succeed; range is adequate without unintended off-site activation; every expected old remote/channel still works or is intentionally revoked; lost/retired credentials fail where revocation was required; memory/audit/admin state matches the plan; photoeyes, sensing edges, obstruction response, stop/reverse, limits, emergency stop, manual release, fire/egress, and mains-loss/backup behavior pass exactly as the operator manual requires. Record date, people, models/serials, results, exceptions, and approval. On any failure, stop, isolate power safely, restore the documented configuration/wiring or reconnect the preserved receiver, and re-run the original-system safety and credential baseline before service. If rollback cannot restore every safety function, keep the system out of service and call a qualified professional.
